source.title: Biomechanical phenotypes of 90° change of direction in football players: Unsupervised machine learning in anterior cruciate ligament injury prevention

paper.citation: Della Villa F., Ghibellini A., Buckthorpe M., Bononi L., Gabbrielli M., Grassi A., et al. Biomechanical phenotypes of 90° change of direction in football players: Unsupervised machine learning in anterior cruciate ligament injury prevention. Knee Surgery, Sports Traumatology, Arthroscopy. 2026;:ksa.70475. doi:10.1002/ksa.70475.
paper.abstract: This paper addresses the following question: Can unsupervised machine learning identify distinct 90° change-of-direction biomechanical phenotypes in a large cohort of healthy young soccer players? Participants: 1,002 competitive soccer players, age 16.3±2.8 years, including 264 females, free from severe musculoskeletal injury. Sport and level: Amateur and professional youth/young-adult soccer, age range 14–21 years. Design: Secondary cross-sectional analysis of the prospective CUTtheACL cohort. Exposure or intervention: Laboratory 90° cuts on artificial turf after warm-up/familiarization.
paper.tldr: Four clusters emerged with silhouette=.43. Cluster sizes were low-force/low-control n=289, low-force/high-control n=242, high-force/low-control n=229, and high-force/high-control n=242. Multivariable clustering can be a useful descriptive layer for organizing complex cutting profiles, but these labels should not trigger ACL-risk classification or individualized “prevention” prescriptions without reliability and prospective-outcome validation.
paper.methods: Design: Secondary cross-sectional analysis of the prospective CUTtheACL cohort. Exposure or intervention: Laboratory 90° cuts on artificial turf after warm-up/familiarization. Comparator: Four data-derived clusters rather than prespecified clinical groups. Measurements and outcomes: Three high-speed cameras, force platform, 2D kinematics, ground-reaction forces, speed/time variables, and Movement Analysis Test scores; 42 normalized biomechanical features entered clustering. Analysis: t-SNE dimensionality reduction, Ward agglomerative clustering, silhouette optimization, ARI stability/consensus analyses, random-forest threefold classification, and between-cluster tests.
paper.findings: Four clusters emerged with silhouette=.43. Cluster sizes were low-force/low-control n=289, low-force/high-control n=242, high-force/low-control n=229, and high-force/high-control n=242. Stability across high perplexities was ARI=.701, stability across random seeds was ARI=.717, and consensus with K-means was ARI=.658. Random-forest cross-validation predicted the cluster labels with precision .91–.95, recall .90–.94, and F1 .91–.94. Peak posterior GRF differed across clusters (1.0±0.3, 0.9±0.2, 1.3±0.3, and 1.5±0.4 N/BW; ηp²=.40, p<.001), illustrating the force dimension used to interpret phenotypes.
paper.limitations: Preplanned 90° cutting may not represent unplanned or varied in-game tasks; no strength or EMG data were collected. The 14–21-year soccer cohort limits transfer to adult professionals or American football. Dimensionality reduction can oversimplify individual strategies; each player was tested once, so phenotype test–retest reliability was unknown. Most importantly, no injury outcome was included; the clusters are descriptive movement phenotypes, not validated ACL-risk categories.
paper.practicalImplications: Multivariable clustering can be a useful descriptive layer for organizing complex cutting profiles, but these labels should not trigger ACL-risk classification or individualized “prevention” prescriptions without reliability and prospective-outcome validation. For collegiate American football, both task and population differ substantially, so any analogous workflow requires sport-specific data and external validation.

For collegiate American football, both task and population differ substantially, so any analogous workflow requires sport-specific data and external validation. Apply the finding within the population and setting described in the source rather than treating it as a universal threshold.
paper.rtp: For rehabilitation and return-to-sport decisions, multivariable clustering can be a useful descriptive layer for organizing complex cutting profiles, but these labels should not trigger ACL-risk classification or individualized “prevention” prescriptions without reliability and prospective-outcome validation. For collegiate American football, both task and population differ substantially, so any analogous workflow requires sport-specific data and external validation. Use the paper as one input to interdisciplinary judgment, not as a standalone clearance criterion or reinjury prediction rule.
